LESSON 67 OF 106·Web and Application Security Basics

Vulnerable and Outdated Components: Knowing What You Depend On

Why a modern application inherits risk it never wrote: what a CVE describes, and how an SBOM turns dependency risk into a list you can act on.

Foundation14 min
Why this matters

The 2021 list called this vulnerable and outdated components. The 2025 list broadened it into software supply chain failures, because the risk is rarely only in a library you chose yourself.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • A dependency you did not write is code you are responsible for, and it is usually a large share of what you ship.
  • A component advisory matters only in context: if the vulnerable function is never called, the practical risk is different.
  • Transitive dependencies mean a vulnerability can arrive through something you never named.
  • A compromised package version is a supply chain attack, and version pinning is what makes it possible.
  • An unmaintained component will never receive a fix, so exposure grows without anyone choosing it.

The background

  • Component reuse accelerated development and quietly transferred a large amount of security responsibility to third parties.
  • Software composition analysis tooling made dependency inventories practical and sharply increased the visible number of findings.
  • Compromised maintainer accounts and malicious package versions turned a maintenance question into a security one.
  • The 2025 list responded by renaming and widening the category to cover the whole chain rather than the library alone.

Real-world examples

  • A widely used library maintainer account is taken over, and every application pulling that version is exposed within hours.
  • An application inherits hundreds of transitive dependencies, and only a generated inventory shows what is actually there.
  • A component used for a single convenience function can be the largest single risk in the build.

What to look for

  • Check whether a machine-readable inventory of dependencies exists and includes transitive components.
  • Check whether advisories are monitored and acted on, and against what prioritisation.
  • Check build pipelines for unpinned versions and for install scripts that execute third-party code.
  • Check whether any component is unmaintained, since those will never be fixed.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

OWASP Software Component Verification Standard

Reading a vendor-neutral standard for verifying software components and assessing a personal project's build and dependency practices against it

Open OWASP resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Generate a dependency inventory in the build and fail the build on new high-severity findings.
  • Pin versions and use lock files, so a build is reproducible and cannot silently pull a new version.
  • Prioritise by reachability: whether the vulnerable code path is actually used in your product.
  • Remove unused dependencies, since a component nobody uses is risk with no benefit.
  • Restrict what build steps and install scripts can do, and monitor upstream sources for new advisories.
